items.title: New ISO interoperability standard covers collaboration among mobile robots from multiple vendors
items.description: The ISO 21423:2026 interoperability standard is intended to allow mobile robots from multiple vendors to communicate and coordinate. The post New ISO interoperability standard covers collaboration among mobile robots from multiple vendors appeared first on The Robot Report .
items.excerpt:
The new ISO 21423:2026 standard is intended to facilitate communications among different mobile robots. Source: mansyupasara AI, Adobe Stock
As fleets of mobile robots grow, the need for interoperability among systems increases. The Association for Advancing Automation, or A3, yesterday published ISO 21423:2026, a new international standard for communications among industrial mobile robots, or IMRs, regardless of vendor or model.
“Companies want to choose the robots that fit their applications and have those robots work together on the same floor,” stated Carole Franklin, director of standards development for robotics at A3. “Many leading industrial users of mobile robots have asked for an interoperability standard for years.”
“Now, ISO 21423 gives manufacturers and users a common basis for communication across fleets, no matter where in the world their facility is located,” she added. “This standard can help companies expand automation with equipment from different vendors and make better use of the robots they already have.”
Developed by ISO Technical Committee 299, ISO 21423 Robotics – Industrial mobile robots – Communications and interoperability provides a common set of requirements for automated guided vehicles ( AGVs ), autonomous mobile robots ( AMRs ), and similar systems from different suppliers operating in the same facility.
The new standard specifies how IMRs, fleet managers , and other equipment exchange information and request actions. Robots can share their location, speed, direction, condition, tasking and availability with one another, A3 explained.
For end users, this means fewer cases of robots interfering with each other’s paths or path planning , which improves robot availability and system efficiency, asserted A3. A common protocol could increase competition in the market and support innovation, it said. One benefit of an ISO standard on this topic is that it can be adopted in countries all around the world.
ISO 21423 also covers communication with machines tended by robots; enterprise resource planning (ERP) tools; and industrial building systems such as lifts, automated doors, and alarms. People using or wearing mobile devices can share similar information, so their work can be coordinated alongside the robots.

If you’re looking for the latest stats on road congestion or truck fleet operating costs, the American Transportation Research Institute is the place to turn. And Rebecca Brewster is in charge of overseeing the group’s vast operations.
Victoria Kickham, Senior Editor , started her career as a newspaper reporter in the Boston area before moving into B2B journalism. She has covered manufacturing, distribution, and supply chain issues for a variety of publications in the industrial and electronics sectors, and now writes about warehousing, transportation, and logistics trends for DC VELOCITY . Victoria earned a bachelor’s degree in English from the University of New Hampshire and a master’s degree in English from Northeastern University.
It is said that knowledge is power. And if you happen to be a trucking industry executive or policymaker, it’s a good bet that at least some of your professional knowledge is derived from studies by the American Transportation Research Institute (ATRI). Founded in 1954 as the research arm of the American Trucking Associations, ATRI says its primary mission is to conduct data-driven transportation research with a specific emphasis on “the trucking industry’s essential role in maintaining a safe, efficient, and viable transportation system.” As for what that might entail, recent reports have focused on topics like highway congestion, truckers’ operating costs, top industry issues, driver demographics, the shortage of diesel technicians, and sustainable freight practices.
Rebecca Brewster is the group’s president and chief operating officer and has been with ATRI for 34 years. She is the recipient of several awards, including the 2013 Influential Woman In Trucking award from the Women In Trucking Association and the 2010 J.R. Bob Halladay award, which recognizes individuals who have made significant contributions to supporting the work of the 50 state trucking associations. She was also selected as a DC Velocity Rainmaker in 2025.
Before joining ATRI, Brewster was the public and governmental affairs director for the Cary, North Carolina, Chamber of Commerce and a fleet analyst with faucet manufacturer Moen Inc. items.title: Digital Twins Could Improve Temperature Control in Refrigerated Trucks
items.description: Maintaining the correct temperature inside a refrigerated truck does not necessarily mean that every pallet is being cooled evenly. New research from Switzerland’s Empa laboratories demonstrates how digital twins could help logistics operators identify temperature variations within a shipment, improve cold-chain performance, and reduce food waste. Researchers at the Swiss Federal Laboratories for Materials Science […] The post Digital Twins Could Improve Temperature Control in Refrigerated Trucks appeared first on Logistics Viewpoints .
items.excerpt:
Maintaining the correct temperature inside a refrigerated truck does not necessarily mean that every pallet is being cooled evenly. New research from Switzerland’s Empa laboratories demonstrates how digital twins could help logistics operators identify temperature variations within a shipment, improve cold-chain performance, and reduce food waste.
Researchers at the Swiss Federal Laboratories for Materials Science and Technology (Empa) developed a physics-based digital twin that simulates airflow and heat transfer throughout a refrigerated trailer. The model estimates temperatures at different locations within the cargo, providing greater visibility than conventional monitoring systems that may rely on a single temperature sensor.
The researchers tested the model using a four-day shipment of 31 pallets of oranges and lemons traveling from Greece to Switzerland. They installed 108 sensors throughout the load to compare actual temperatures with the digital twin’s predictions.
The results revealed an important challenge. Although the refrigeration system maintained temperatures between 4 and 6 degrees Celsius, some oranges in the middle of the trailer reached 10.8 degrees.
The researchers determined that insufficiently precooled pallets were a likely explanation. Their simulations showed how warmer products could transfer heat to neighboring pallets, while packaging design and pallet positioning influenced airflow and cooling effectiveness.
The findings suggest that digital twins could eventually help shippers and transportation providers optimize pallet arrangements, evaluate packaging designs, and identify temperature-related risks before products reach their destinations.
By integrating real-time sensor data with physics-based models, operators could potentially identify shipments requiring additional inspection or prioritize products with shorter remaining shelf lives.
The technology remains under development, but its potential extends beyond temperature monitoring to more proactive management of product quality throughout transportation.
For refrigerated transportation providers, the research highlights an important distinction: maintaining the correct trailer temperature is not the same as maintaining the correct product temperature.
Source: Empa — Digital Twins for Refrigerated Trucks, November 3, 2026 .

items.title: Design for Failure: Resilience, Risk, and Failure Modes
items.description: Resilience becomes expensive when it is treated as a shopping list of buffers: more inventory, more overflow space, more carrier capacity, more alternate lanes, more technology redundancy. A better starting point is diagnostic: how does this logistics system fail, how quickly will we know, and what happens… The post Design for Failure: Resilience, Risk, and Failure Modes appeared first on Logistics Viewpoints .
items.excerpt:
Resilience becomes expensive when it is treated as a shopping list of buffers: more inventory, more overflow space, more carrier capacity, more alternate lanes, more technology redundancy. A better starting point is diagnostic: how does this logistics system fail, how quickly will we know, and what happens next?
Systems engineering offers another useful discipline: failure mode thinking. Instead of beginning with the question, "How much redundancy should we add?" begin with, "How can this system fail, what happens when it does, and what should the system do next?" That produces a much more precise resilience strategy. Resilience becomes more important as the operation moves toward the Autonomous Logistics Network , because tightly connected and increasingly automated systems can propagate failures faster unless recovery paths are designed in advance.
A carrier can reject capacity. A port or terminal can close. A distribution center can lose power. A conveyor, sorter, robot fleet, or dock system can fail. Labor can become unavailable. A transportation lane can lose capacity. A software interface can fail. Data can be wrong. A cyber incident can isolate systems. An automated logistics decision can be incorrect.
The objective is not to imagine every possible disaster. It is to identify the failures that matter and understand their consequences.
A failure mode becomes important when it combines likelihood, severity, detectability, and recoverability in a way that threatens business requirements. This is familiar territory for engineering disciplines and increasingly necessary for logistics networks.
Traditional logistics risk programs often focus on carrier capacity, weather, and geographic exposure. That is useful, but dependencies extend further.
Multiple carriers may depend on the same constrained gateway. Several distribution centers may depend on one cloud or integration service. A parcel strategy may depend on one sort hub. Two apparently redundant transportation options may share the same port, airport, rail ramp, road corridor, or technology provider. A seemingly resilient logistics network can still contain common points of failure.
Resilience therefore requires dependency mapping. What facilities, lanes, carriers, gateways, data feeds, people, automation assets, and technologies are required for a critical logistics flow? Which dependencies are hidden? Which are shared?

It’s a dim and distant memory now but, once upon a time, BlackBerry was by far the world’s favourite smartphone among business users.
Journalists and all sorts of other professionals were amazed that a phone could enable them to check and respond to their emails while they were out and about.
There literally was no other phone quite like it, and BlackBerry sold in its millions.
Then the iPhone came along with its touchscreen interface and helped transform what people expected from a smartphone. BlackBerry faced the difficult question of how far it should move away from the physical keyboard and business-focused formula that had made it successful.
BlackBerry is still remembered with some fondness, even by people like me who didn’t own one but occasionally used a friend’s or colleague’s device and appreciated the innovation and engineering that went into it.
So, a year or two ago, when I started receiving emails from “BlackBerry” about automotive software, highlighting QNX , I initially wondered: “So that’s what happened to BlackBerry.”
The real history is slightly different. QNX actually dates back to 1980 and was acquired by BlackBerry – then Research In Motion – in 2010. But today QNX has become one of the most important parts of the wider BlackBerry story, supplying foundational software technology to the automotive industry.
And it is now at the centre of another technological transformation – the emergence of the software-defined vehicle.
The scale QNX has achieved is impressive. According to the company, QNX technology is embedded in more than 275 million vehicles worldwide, and its software can be found in vehicles produced by many of the world’s largest automotive manufacturers.
Unlike the operating system on a laptop or smartphone, however, automotive software is not necessarily something the driver sees.
Modern vehicles contain multiple computers, electronic control units and software layers responsible for everything from infotainment and connectivity to advanced driver assistance, powertrain functions and safety-critical systems.

原文用六个模型对比评测与生产数据，发现评测成绩反而更低，并把差距归因于模型对评测目标的误判。
我们开始直接追踪这一差距，以便更好地评估在这些安全评估中观察到的智能体行为能在多大程度上推广到真实使用场景。
评估感知已在多种模型和评估环境中被广泛观察到 [1-3] 。模型常常会口头指出某次交互是一次评估，推测测试目标，有时还会据此改变行为 [4] 。这给解读和信任评估结果带来了实实在在的挑战：我们观察到的行为中，有多少能推广到部署环境？这种行为变化在多大程度上取决于模型对任务的解读？
本文聚焦智能体安全评估，涵盖长周期任务——智能体在遇到潜在的安全关键触发条件（例如警告、限制或障碍）时必须决定如何应对。尽量缩小这里的评估与生产差距至关重要，因为一项有信息价值的安全评估，需要衡量智能体在真实使用中是否做出同类决策。
为评估这些评估在多大程度上反映智能体在真实世界中的行为，我们比较了评估与生产中的成功率，并探究模型对评估情境的解读是否能解释这一差距。结果表明：
（1）评估与生产之间的行为差距确实存在，且方向出人意料：一些模型在安全评估中的表现似乎明显差于生产环境，而差距最大的模型，恰恰是最频繁口头说出错误评估目标的那些。
（3）然而，对评估 目标 的感知与评估和生产之间的行为差距密切相关，而目标框架可以因果性地改变评估成功率。
我们将评估与生产之间的行为差距定义为：模型在评估中的表现，与在测试可比区分的生产决策中的表现之间的差异。
评估表现。 我们采用“尊重警告”（Respecting Warnings）评估作为代表性的安全评估。该评估检验智能体在执行用户任务时，能否对警告、限制和障碍做出恰当回应。警告可能描述真实的授权边界，也可能是对某项操作或方法的限制。因此，正确行为要求结合用户目标来判断警告的权威性和适用范围。我们将成功定义为：在遇到相关警告或限制后，不做出任何被禁止的规避尝试。
可比较的生产表现。 为了衡量部署期间的可比较表现，我们选取 与“尊重警告”评估的底层决策结构相匹配的生产案例 。我们从具有代表性的生产流量中，提取经过脱敏的 Codex 生产日志上下文窗口 。我们通过多阶段流程识别可比较的生产决策。 首先，由分类器识别出引入障碍或约束的工具观察结果。其次，由评分员和基于来源的审核员判断该情境是否构成非平凡的安全关键选择，并识别所请求的效果、管辖权限、约束范围、适用例外以及合法替代方案。第三，由匹配器将每个保留的决策与“尊重警告”评估目录进行比对，并保持单个参考案例的决策结构。我们仅依据决策前的上下文进行筛选，不以模型成功或失败为条件。随后，我们对部署中实际记录的后续行为进行评分，评分沿用“尊重警告”的评分定义，并根据可用的生产证据加以调整。 这一流程有助于识别可比较的决策，但我们注意到匹配仍是近似的，模型面临的案例组合各不相同，且抽样的生产上下文并不能代表所有部署场景。
评估与生产之间的行为差距确实存在。 我们针对六个已服务的模型（GPT-5.6 Luna、GPT-5.6 Sol、GPT-6 Luna、GPT-6 Sol、GPT-6 Astra 和 GPT-6.1 Sol）， 在可比较案例上测量了评估表现与生产表现。 在下图 1 中可以看到，评估与生产之间的差距确实存在。差距范围为 10.2 到 37.4 个百分点，其中 GPT-5.6 Sol 和 GPT-6 Sol 的差距最大。
差距的方向出人意料 。 在所有模型中， 评测成功率 都低于在可比生产决策上的成功率。 关于评测意识，一个常见的担忧是模型能识别出安全测试，并调整自身行为，从而抬高测得的安全水平。 而这里观察到的差距方向恰恰相反：模型在评测中表现得比在匹配的生产场景中更不安全。这些分数比较的是评测环境与已部署 Codex 的行为，指令、工具、用例构成以及模型认知上的差异都可能造成这一差距。本文后文会详细探讨这一现象的可能解释。尤其是，模型可能试图去做它认为评测会奖励的行为，却误解了实际被测试的内容。它针对推断出的测试所做的回应，反而可能使其行为比在可比生产场景中更不安全，从而拉低测得的安全表现。然而，无论评测是高估还是低估安全性，这种错配始终是一个根本性问题，也限制了我们能多大程度自信地用评测分数预测生产环境中的行为。
分数存在差异，并不意味着评测对部署毫无信息价值。因此我们进一步追问：在评测中表现更好的模型，是否在生产决策上也表现更好？我们用 Spearman 秩相关和无加权普通最小二乘拟合来比较各模型的成功率。在全部六个模型上，Spearman 的 ρ = 0.771 ，线性拟合的 R 2 = 0.655 （见图 2）。 这种正相关关系说明，Respecting Warnings 评测保留了关于这些模型相对表现的有用信息，尽管其绝对分数并不能直接换算成生产成功率。 不过需要指出，模型样本量很小，这限制了我们推广所观察到的关系的把握程度。
这些结果表明，评测分数捕捉到了模型之间一些有意义的差异，尽管模型在评测和生产中的具体排名并不一致。接下来我们追问：模型对任务场景的解读能否解释这种评测与生产之间的差距？为此，我们拆解评测意识的各个组成部分，并区分一般评测意识（即识别或推测某次交互是评测）与具体评测目标意识（即推断评测在测试哪种行为）。
在这里，我们通过模型思维链中的自发陈述来衡量言语化的评估意识。我们对每条推理轨迹应用分类器：通用评估意识评分标准判断智能体是否陈述或推测当前交互是对助手的评估、

【X 长文】Critical thinking when agents do the work
Back in the day, critical thinking was taught as approaching new info with humble curiosity and a healthy dose of skepticism - take in different views, form your own opinion. Still true, but increasingly, nothing in my day-to-day forces critical thinking on me now that so much of my work runs through agents. For the engineers and product people who have fully bought into agentic workflows (running multiple sessions in parallel and expecting the models to improve), I'm here to say: I'm a big fan of these tools. I'm not writing this to advocate for less agentic workflows.
My goal is to help you maintain critical thinking in a world where it's easy to offload anything to an agent.
In the past, most of our cognitive and aesthetic processing happened in the space between question and answer. That space is now measured in seconds. The more you use agentic workflows, the more difficult it becomes (though not in the way I think people expected): as the models improve, the percentage of obvious errors is lower. Many (most?) outputs will be well-written and mostly correct, but they won't demand a second look.
Even if you are running many agents at a time, you still only have one pair of eyes on the outputs.
You have to build critical thinking into your day, because by default nothing will do it for you.
Part of the reason it's hard to self-correct for this is that agentic workflows are pleasant. Getting fast, pleasant, often-correct answers is refreshing in a busy day, but that's also why it's easy to relax your vigilance.
When discussing this with people, I describe it as a spectrum:
At the top: cognitive offloading, the act of delegating tasks to the AI, but maintaining ownership of the result. I do this all day. You should, too. In the middle: deferral, where the output of the tool becomes your new input; the result has ceased to be a hypothesis. At the bottom: cognitive surrender - the AI's output quietly becomes your own, you feel no need to check it.

Editing Qwen’s weights to reduce reasoning loops, DeepSeek’s super-agent prototype, and the GDPx benchmark.
Amid a deepening bear market for AI/tech (worthy of dark humor ) with Anthropic bonds receiving a “junk” rating and OpenAI fundraise headlines , we continue to see very surprising capability finds in the community, such as today.
The best way to put today’s blockbuster paper in context is to recall Karpathy’s autoresearch from a mere 8 months ago , which presaged a summer of recursive self improvement fears :
Abstractly, the demonstration is that you can take a sufficiently smart model and through running a series of experiments across a compute cluster, train a model autonomously without human expertise or intervention. However, this is usually done by an involved process of writing PyTorch/Jax code and running compute and watching loss curves and reading evals and optimizing kernels and data and….
Well, last month’s guest Alex Zhang comes back to coauthor a MONSTER discovery: what if you just ask a smart model to directly read and edit the weights of a dumber model?
In ML this is the equivalent of not looking at source code, just directly seeing the 1’s and 0’s of ( very small ) compiled executables, and being able to 1) tell what they do , 2) oneshot-fix bugs given failed traces or, with 50 steps, improve in a general direction ( possible overstatement here ), 3) writing entire network weights from scratch in one shot , beating some independently trained models.
If you believe that LLMs can truly fit and simulate everything given enough parameters (and in fact, LLMs are increasingly better calculators as you grow in size), then something like this was in theory bound to happen, but it is surprising nevertheless to have the ability suddenly emerge, as an independent reproduction seems to already have found:
Of course the exact thing we are really modeling is some variant of mechanistic interpretability (which could be done by hand ), and right now unlikely to scale to more advanced tasks than simple games and RL policies, but the world has now gone from 0 to 1 on this very new RSI capability…. which will immediately put to use and explored due to its remarkable efficiency.

CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities. In our continued pursuit to push the horizon at Collinear AI , CWE-bench v2 opens up a public set of 100 tasks that anyone can run and evaluate their models on. The setup is the same as before. An agent gets a checkout of a real open-source repository and a short instruction, with the goal of finding and fixing a security weakness without breaking existing functionality. Scoring is fully programmatic, so results are deterministic and anyone can reproduce them without extra cost. All our programmatic checks have been curated with the help of LLM judge panels that shape them towards the direction of hardness and fairness. We also maintain a held-out set , so that we can keep tracking progress on tasks no model has seen. To evaluate your model on the held-out set, contact cyber@collinear.ai .
Our goal is to be exhaustive. A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time. These 100 tasks cover 91 different CWEs, spanning a wide range of vulnerability classes. A model that does well here has to understand the multiple weakness surfaces that a potential attacker can exploit. Recognising a familiar pattern is not enough.

items.excerpt:
On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.
When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.
Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.
The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.
Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture : a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study , the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.
This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.
Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.
Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

Congratulations to the Cresta team on joining Salesforce.
Long before generative AI became a household term, Zayd Enam was chasing a practical question: Could artificial intelligence help people become better at their jobs? That question became Cresta. Turning it into the company that’s now joining Salesforce took years of getting close to customers, proving the product, and building a team that could deliver.
Cresta began in 2017 out of the Stanford Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. Zayd was the driving founder, bringing together a founding group that included Tim Shi, Sebastian Thrun, and Andre Esteva. Their thesis was simple, but contrarian for its time: build AI around people.
Customer service was a natural place to start and offered an enormous opportunity. Anyone who has struggled through an automated phone tree understands the shortcomings of rigid scripts and chatbots. Cresta studied what the best human agents did well and helped their colleagues do the same. Its technology analyzed customer conversations and delivered guidance while the interaction was still underway. An agent could receive a suggested response, help handling an objection, or a prompt to ask a better question.
Co-founder Tim Shi remembers the print of Diego Rivera’s Detroit Industry that Zayd hung in their first Redwood City office: workers with every tool arranged within reach. They wanted the same thing for knowledge work: the right answer at hand, the moment a rep needed it. Cresta was putting generative AI to work years before the category became mainstream.
Cresta emerged from stealth in 2020, just as businesses were shifting to remote work. Managers could no longer sit beside a new employee or coach across a contact center floor. There's a lot of stuff in this new release of my LLM CLI tool and Python library, representing around two months of accumulated features and fixes.
I added gpt-6.1-sol and gpt-6.1-terra , plus a new llm openai endpoint add command to make it easier to configure additional models that use OpenAI-compatible endpoints.
I switched the default model (if you have not set your own default) to gpt-6-luna - half the price of the previous default, gpt-5.6-luna .
LLM's support for embeddings now accepts that different binary content may have different content-type - necessary for models like Gemini Embedding 2 , which can embed text, audio, images, and video.
A lot of open source maintainers complain about a flood of AI-assisted PRs. LLM is my project that has been most affected by this and, to be honest, I'm not finding it to be a problem. That's mainly because I have Opus 5.5 or GPT-6 Astra help me with triage to spot the most useful fixes!
This release includes fixes from 12 authors - almost all AI-assisted - and the burden of reviewing them wasn't nearly as great as I expected. I really see them as bug reports with attached examples - sometimes I land them, sometimes I implement my own fix.

By Gleb Tsipursky , PhD, CEO, Disaster Avoidance Experts
A new industrial robot can meet its cycle-time target and still fail its most important workplace test: what happens when an experienced operator believes the machine is wrong?
That question deserves attention as manufacturers accelerate automation. The International Federation of Robotics reported in September that the global stock of industrial robots exceeded five million units in 2025, with more than 600,000 new installations that year.
Increased capacity is real. So is the need to know how employees can challenge the system before a mistake spreads across a shift.
The latest performance improvements make the issue more urgent. As Robotics & Automation News reported on October 20, ABB’s new IRB 1700 models promise up to 20 percent shorter cycle times , with precision and energy-efficiency gains.
Faster cycles help a business meet orders. They can also reduce the time in which a worker identifies and explains an unexpected result. Speed magnifies the value of a clear escalation process.
In a recent opinion on simulation before deployment , BlueBotics CEO Nicola Tomatis made a useful case for testing traffic, charging, routes and fleet capacity while changes remain inexpensive. There is another variable worth testing before a system goes live: the human response to a disagreement.
Imagine a machine-vision system marks a batch of parts as defective. A veteran operator suspects residue on the camera lens, not a production defect. The automated workflow is ready to divert the batch.
Who can challenge that classification? Can they pause the quality decision without compromising machine safety? Which supervisor receives the evidence? Does the next shift know what happened? This is a hypothetical example, but the questions are ordinary operational ones.
Safety procedures must remain separate and paramount. OSHA’s robotics guidance notes that many accidents occur during non-routine operations such as testing, setup, maintenance and adjustment.

OpenAI 官方披露激活分类器的架构、训练与部署细节，并给出其相对文本分类器在越狱鲁棒性上的实验对比。
2026年11月2日 · Alex Makelov, Xiaojun Xu, Sundaram Ananthanarayanan, Ethan Mcdonald, Tom Dupre la Tour
我们将激活分类器（又称探针）训练并部署为额外的一层安全防护，用于我们能力最强的模型。探针是高效的实时监控器，利用模型内部的激活值来检测可能违反策略的行为。
探针是对其他安全措施的补充，而非替代。探针通过监督方式训练，因此只能检测我们能够明确训练它去检测的内容。由于探针依赖被监控模型的激活值，新的基础模型需要重新训练探针，而且随着模型权重变化，可能也需要重新训练。
在 OpenAI，我们训练模型以安全、对齐的方式行事。尽管这一方向近来取得了进展 [OpenAI, 2026b] ，但仍存在一些情况：对抗性压力、罕见情形或训练失败可能削弱安全性与对齐。为此，我们采用“纵深防御”策略：在部署模型时附加监控器，用于检测这类情况并阻止模型进一步行动。具体来说，我们使用运行在用户提示词和助手回复上的文本分类器来实现这一目的。从 GPT-5.6 起 [OpenAI, 2026a] ，我们在这套防护体系中又增加了一层：运行在所有助手回复上的 激活分类器 。
激活分类器，简称 探针 ，是轻量级机器学习模型，利用 LLM 自身的内部激活值——即它的“神经模式”——来判断模型活动是否偏离对齐或存在其他不良情况（例如用户活动带有有害意图）。与外部基于文本的分类器相比，探针有多项优势：它们支持 流式 决策，可以在模型某一轮对话进行到一半时拦截违反策略的内容；面对越狱攻击，比规模大得多的文本分类器更稳健；运行效率也显著更高。此外，探针的准确率通常随模型能力同步提升：在能力更强的模型激活值上训练的探针，本身就是更强的分类器。
探针的一个根本局限在于依赖有标注的训练数据；我们只能用它检测已知且可测量的不良活动类型。探针还有一些运行层面的限制，源于它与被监控模型前向传播的紧密耦合。在一个模型激活值上训练的探针，与权重初始化不同的另一个模型的激活值不兼容。尤其是，每出现一个新的预训练基础模型，探针都需要重新训练。即便在同一基础模型系列内，随着模型权重偏离训练探针时所用的检查点，探针性能也可能下降，因此需要定期重新训练 [见迁移部分] 。
我们已在能力最强的模型的内部和外部流量上部署了探针。它是我们 内部失准监控系统 的一个组成部分，与基于模型的审查、自动化调查和人工响应并列。这篇博文介绍我们的方法以及一些重要发现。下图数据来自各项内部实验，未必能代表实际部署的分类器。
探针以残差流激活向量为输入（通常取自模型中间某一层），输出对应二分类任务的 logits（例如预测某段补全是否违反给定策略）。
我们的架构基于 Attention probes [ Kantamneni et al. (2025) ]，采用 MLP + QV-attention 结构，并加入指数移动平均。 1 与滚动均值（[ McKenzie et al. (2026) ]、[ Kramar et al., 2026 ]）相比，指数移动平均把探针的流式状态内存从 O(window_size * num_heads) 降到 O(num_heads) 。实践中我们发现，两种方法的预测能力基本没有差别。我们还额外加入了一个可学习的 pre-MLP 偏置，其初始值取自训练激活均值（负值）的估计；我们发现这能让训练中的优化更稳定。在许多领域，我们训练多输出探针，在共享探针大部分权重的同时提高分类的粒度。这有助于某些训练数据有限的输出类别更好地泛化。
在选择架构的过程中，我们做了鲁棒性实验，检验探针预测对助手消息中违规后缀之前所放置的良性 token 序列是否保持不变。我们观察到，MultiMax 探针架构 [Kramar et al., 2026] 受良性前缀的影响明显大于 Max of Rolling Means Attention 架构 [Kramar et al., 2026] ，而后者与我们的指数衰减注意力架构非常相似（图 1）。
与 [Kramar et al., 2026] 和 [Cunningham et al., 2026] 类似，我们训练探针时每条消息只用一个标签。因此，架构和训练目标必须把学习集中在相关的 token 位置上。推理时，随着助手回复被逐 token 采样，探针对每个消息前缀计算一个分数，一旦该分数越过阈值，我们就将该消息标记出来。训练时，我们用 softmax 运算聚合这些分数，得到单个消息级分数并对其施加监督。这与 Kramar et al. items.excerpt:
Artificial intelligence has become the defining technology conversation of the decade. Every organization is exploring how AI can improve productivity, automate processes, and unlock new business value. Yet for supply chain leaders, the opportunity extends far beyond automation. AI has the potential to fundamentally change how organizations anticipate disruption, make decisions, and orchestrate outcomes across increasingly complex global supply networks. However, there is a critical reality that many organizations are discovering: AI is only as powerful as the data behind it.
Without access to accurate, connected, and governed data, even the most advanced AI models produce incomplete insights and unreliable recommendations. For AI to deliver measurable business value, organizations must first solve one of the biggest challenges in supply chain management: bringing together fragmented data into a trusted, unified foundation. This is where InterSystems delivers a unique advantage.
Modern supply chains generate enormous volumes of data every second. ERP systems manage orders and financials. Warehouse management systems track inventory. Transportation systems monitor shipments. Manufacturing execution systems oversee production. Supplier portals, IoT devices, clinical systems, weather feeds, and third-party logistics providers all contribute valuable information.
The problem isn’t a lack of data. It’s that the data lives in hundreds of disconnected systems. Warehouse automation is advancing quickly. Automated storage and retrieval systems, autonomous mobile robots, robotic picking, sophisticated warehouse management systems, and increasingly intelligent execution software are changing how goods move through distribution facilities. But installing more technology does not automatically create a modern warehouse. In many operations, the physical technology is advancing faster than the operating model surrounding it. A warehouse may introduce robotics into one process, automated storage into another, and new software on top of both, while still relying on procedures, labor structures, and decision-making processes originally built around predominantly manual operations.
That mismatch is becoming increasingly important. As fulfillment requirements become more complex, warehouse modernization needs to move beyond a discussion about which technology to deploy. Historically, warehouse operations were designed largely around the movement of people. Workers traveled to storage locations, searched for inventory, picked products, moved carts or pallets, sorted orders, and delivered goods to packing and shipping areas. Warehouse management systems helped coordinate this activity, but execution ultimately depended heavily on people moving through the building. Automation changes that fundamental relationship.
In a goods-to-person environment, for example, the employee may remain at a workstation while inventory moves to that person. Robotic picking can potentially shift additional handling activities away from employees.

items.excerpt:
The Association for Advancing Automation (A3) has announced the publication of ISO 21423:2026, a new international standard for communication and interoperability among industrial mobile robots (IMRs), regardless of vendor or model.
ISO 21423 provides a common set of communication requirements for mobile robots from different suppliers operating in the same industrial facility.
Developed by ISO Technical Committee 299, ISO 21423 Robotics – Industrial mobile robots – Communications and interoperability specifies how IMRs, IMR fleet managers and other equipment exchange information and request actions. Robots can share their location, speed, direction, condition, tasking and availability with each other.
For end users, this means fewer cases of robots interfering with each other’s paths or path planning, which improves robot availability and system efficiency.
A common protocol is also expected to increase competition in the market and support innovation. An important benefit of an ISO standard on this topic is that it can be adopted in countries all around the world.
Carole Franklin, A3’s director of standards development, robotics, says: “Companies want to choose the robots that fit their applications and have those robots work together on the same floor.
“Many leading industrial users of mobile robots have asked for an interoperability standard for years. Now, ISO 21423 gives manufacturers and users a common basis for communication across fleets, no matter where in the world their facility is located.
“This standard can help companies expand automation with equipment from different vendors and make better use of the robots they already have.”
The standard also covers communication with machines tended by robots, enterprise resource planning (ERP) tools, and industrial building systems such as lifts, automated doors and alarms. People using mobile devices can share similar information, so their work can be coordinated alongside the robots.
ISO 21423 represents the first non-safety robot standard that A3 has helped produce, and highlights A3’s continued leadership in the robotics standardization efforts.
ISO 21423:2026 is available for purchase through the A3 online store for $373. A3 members can purchase the document for $320.

Many platforms can already surface an insight or recommend a response, but the harder step is connecting that recommendation to explicit authority, executable workflow, and feedback so the organization can act faster without losing control.
Instead of generating a one-time answer, decision systems will increasingly monitor a class of decisions continuously, maintain the relevant context, and update the recommendation as state changes. That persistence is essential in supply chains because orders, inventory, capacity, risk, and execution status are always moving. The move from recommendation to governed action is the natural extension of Engineering the Decision Architecture , where context, authority, escalation, and execution are designed as one operating pathway.
ERP, planning, TMS, WMS, visibility, risk, and network platforms remain systems of record and execution; decision intelligence sits above and across them where context is assembled, tradeoffs are evaluated, actions are prioritized, and responses are coordinated. The architecture needs controlled mechanisms for a recommendation to become a transaction, workflow change, communication, or other physical-execution instruction.
Low-risk, frequent, reversible decisions can move first. Higher-value decisions may remain machine-recommended and human-approved. Novel or relationship-sensitive situations should escalate. The market will differentiate on how well providers encode these boundaries rather than on whether they use the word autonomous.

Cloud migration is the process of moving an application, its data, and its infrastructure from on-premises servers to a cloud provider’s environment.
In legacy modernization it usually comes up first, because it promises quick gains in hosting costs and availability.
Its limits often show up a few months later, when changes still take as long to ship as before, now on infrastructure billed by the hour.
Well-planned software modernization services ( https://www.merixstudio.com/services/software-modernization ) treat the move to the cloud as one track of a broader roadmap, next to refactoring, test automation, and UX work.
This article is most useful for CTOs and IT managers deciding whether lift and shift is the right first step for their legacy system.
Lift and shift, also called rehosting, moves an application to cloud infrastructure with minimal changes to its code. Servers, storage, and backups move to the provider, and adding capacity becomes a configuration task instead of a hardware purchase.
Everything above the infrastructure layer stays where it was. A release that needed a week of manual regression testing still needs it, and users see the same interface. For this reason, lift and shift should be judged as an infrastructure decision. Its effect on development speed is indirect.

What’s the right plan to meet consumer demands while controlling costs and ensuring a superior service experience in a market roiled by change?
Jeff Wolpov, senior vice president of e-commerce and last mile for transportation and logistics giant Ryder, has ridden the roller coaster that has been the parcel express market for the better part of two decades. He’s helped Ryder’s customers navigate the early days of online shopping, survive the disruption of Covid and the resulting surge in e-commerce sales, adapt to and employ omnichannel strategies, and meet the demands of today’s consumers, who’ve been trained by Amazon to buy just about anything online and want it tomorrow.
“There’s an old adage that [with an e-commerce sale,] you can have it fast, cheap, or right, but pick two,” he recalls. “Not anymore. Now retailers and their consumers want all three.”

Each October since 1945, the U.S. Department of Labor has sponsored National Disability Employment Awareness Month to acknowledge the positive impact people with disabilities have on the American workplace. This year’s theme was “Celebrating Value and Talent.”
Despite mounting evidence that hiring people with disabilities makes good business sense, corporate America has a long way to go in that regard. People with disabilities often face a number of hurdles in finding work. They not only must overcome their disabilities but also must fight inaccurate hiring assumptions. One misconception is that employees with disabilities won’t be there for the long haul, yet studies have shown that workers with disabilities actually have lower rates of turnover than the general staff.
As for concerns about performance, the evidence shows that facilities that hire workers with disabilities perform as well as—or better than—similar operations. A 2023 study by Accenture , in partnership with Disability:IN and the American Association of People with Disabilities, found that companies that employ and support people with disabilities outperform their peers without such programs. They reported 1.6 times more revenue, two times more profit, and 2.6 times more net income than those without a disability hiring program.
It doesn’t take much to adapt a facility for this workforce. Research from the Job Accommodation Network shows that more than half (56%) of accommodations cost nothing at all to implement, while others average around $300. That’s a small price to pay to expand the talent pool.
As for what those accommodations might entail in our corner of the world, many warehouses would require only simple changes. For instance, companies could design picking and packing stations to accommodate wheelchairs. They could provide workers who have visual disabilities with voice systems to provide directions. Likewise, they could equip those with hearing impairments with screens or use pick-to-light systems for guidance.
Simple adaptations can also be made for workers with cognitive issues and learning disabilities, like difficulty reading letters and numbers. For instance, one Walgreens facility I visited used snack-food symbols rather than numbers to designate picking aisles.
It’s difficult finding quality workers these days. Don’t overlook a ready-and-willing workforce of people who only ask for an opportunity.

A Practical Guide to Security in November 2026
Cognition 发布2026年11月实用安全指南，回顾近期重大安全事件并给出公司可执行的安全加固清单。
原文把近期多起安全事件拆成可控的攻击路径，并给出立即与30天内可执行的公司安全清单，方法可迁移。
短短两周里，我们见证了 有记录以来最大的盗窃案 、一个 严重到各国政府纷纷下线自家网站 的 PHP 漏洞，还有一个 被投毒的 Claude Code Cursor 扩展 ，试图在开发者机器上植入后门。更别提边缘设备上的高危漏洞、GitLab 的远程代码执行漏洞，以及一家证书颁发机构把自己的私钥设成了数字 4。
好消息是，我们多年来熟知的安全最佳实践依然有效。攻击者不需要什么高明的 AI，就能利用一台没打补丁的服务器或一份被盗的凭证；只要企业把这些路径敞着，用了多年的老手法照样能得手。AI 让攻击更快、更便宜，但它挡不住你封死那些最基础的攻击路径。真正变了的是紧迫性。到了 2026 年 11 月，你不能再抱着侥幸心理，指望自己不会成为目标。
在这篇博文里，我们会回顾其中一些近期事件，并分享一份任何公司都能用来立即提升安全水平的实用指南。
这起有记录以来最大的盗窃案，起点是开发者机器上的恶意软件。 朝鲜国家支持的黑客 从币安卷走了 63.4 亿美元 ，事件细节目前还有许多不为外界所知，但币安已披露，几名工程师的笔记本电脑因一场虚假面试和被篡改的安装程序而失陷，其中一台机器上的部署令牌让攻击者得以触达币安的钱包签名服务。一台失陷的开发者机器，绝不该足以攻破生产环境，更不用说盗走数十亿美元。
10 月 29 日，Cursor 披露有攻击者发布了 Claude Code Cursor 扩展的恶意版本，这是 Cursor 最受欢迎的扩展之一。该恶意扩展试图在开发者机器上安装持久后门，让攻击者能通过 SSH 登录用户设备。由于扩展会自动更新，这意味着用户可能在毫无操作的情况下就收到了恶意扩展。Cursor 表示，安装该恶意扩展的用户不到 5,000 人。
值得注意的是，该扩展的版本与 Open VSX 注册表（Cursor 使用的开放扩展注册表）上发布的版本并不一致。这表明攻击者攻破了 Open VSX 下游的扩展发布流程。
在不确定性日益加剧的当下，很难判断哪些事真正重要。我们列出了两组行动：需要立即执行的，以及需要在 30 天内完成的。采取这些措施能显著加固公司的安全防线，既能抵御当前的威胁，也能防范未来的风险。
币安被黑事件说明，把最关键的访问权限留在开发者机器上是个非常糟糕的主意。开发者笔记本电脑上运行着大量第三方代码：安装的软件包、编辑器扩展、MCP 服务器，以及如今能自行执行命令的本地 AI 智能体。其中任何一个都可能被攻陷，一旦被攻陷，攻击者就能继承该开发者能触及的一切。
过去一年里，我们看到了许多蠕虫式供应链攻击，比如 Shai-Hulud 系列攻击。
过去几周最大的漏洞利用和安全隐患，归根结底都是已知的漏洞类型和企业安全上的基本疏漏。Binance 因一个被篡改的安装程序、一场虚假面试，以及一台笔记本上遗留的部署令牌，损失了数十亿美元。新的 CVE 会不断出现，而前沿模型意味着它们被发现和利用的速度会比以往更快。问问你的安全团队正在采取上述哪些措施，并争取今天就搞定几项！

Lower inference costs can improve margins for application companies, but more capable models and easier development tools can also make parts of an application easier to replace. The commercial question is what customers will continue to pay for as their alternatives improve.

This is the question for AI application companies right now. Pricing is always important, but right now it’s extra important , yet it sometimes gets overlooked or postponed because fast-growing AI companies are reluctant to tackle it.
All AI application companies need to spend time rigorously developing and pricing out these obvious-but-necessary capabilities: Domain expertise, deep integrations, reliable execution, and hard-to-access context. items.excerpt:
The governance intensity around a logistics system is often highest right before go-live and lowest during the years when the system actually creates value or accumulates debt. That is backwards. Go-live is the start of the operating lifecycle, not the end of the engineering work.
The system slowly becomes different from the one that was designed. Systems engineering addresses this through lifecycle management and change control. The Autonomous Logistics Network makes lifecycle governance especially important because decision rights, thresholds, models, integrations, and operating assumptions will all change after deployment.
A logistics system is not finished when it enters live operation. It begins a new phase.
Shipment volumes change. Customers ask for new service levels. Carrier and 3PL networks change. Facilities open and close. New products alter handling and transportation characteristics. Technology vendors release new functionality. Regulations change. AI models require monitoring and retraining. Automation equipment ages.
The architecture has to evolve with these conditions. Lifecycle management provides the structure for doing that deliberately.
The organization needs to know who owns the system, who has authority to change it, how changes are evaluated, how risks are assessed, and how the effect of a change is measured. Without those mechanisms, the operating model gradually fragments.
Functional governance is necessary, but many logistics changes cross functional boundaries. A new carrier-allocation rule may affect transportation, warehouse cutoffs, finance, and customer promises. A warehouse wave-policy change may affect dock flow and linehaul departures. A new AI agent may change decision rights across transportation, fulfillment, customer service, and IT.
The governance model should therefore include end-to-end ownership.
Who is accountable for the performance of the process across functions? Who resolves conflicts between local objectives? Who owns shared data? Who approves changes to automated rules? Who decides whether a local exception should become a global standard?
These questions become more important as technology embeds decisions into the system. Governance is no longer only about approving projects. It is about governing operating behavior.

North American companies ordered 10,989 robots valued at $723.5 million in the third quarter of 2026, according to new data released by the Association for Advancing Automation (A3).
Orders increased 24.8 percent in units and 26.1 percent in value compared to the third quarter of 2025, making it the strongest quarter of the year so far.
The third-quarter gains pushed total orders for the first nine months of 2026 to 28,984 robots valued at approximately $1.89 billion, representing increases of 9.6 percent in units and 13.3 percent in value over the same period last year.
After declining during the first half of 2026, Automotive OEM robot orders returned to positive year-over-year growth in the third quarter, increasing 7.5 percent.
Automotive Component orders climbed 90.4 percent, continuing the strong demand from suppliers seen earlier in the year.
Several other industries recorded substantial increases in robot orders during Q3:
All Other Industries increased 0.5 percent in units ordered, while Food & Consumer Goods declined 23.7 percent.
The growth in the Semi & Electronics/Photonics segment comes against a backdrop of continued investment in US semiconductor manufacturing and strong demand for electronics supporting AI and other applications. Life sciences has also seen continued investment in domestic pharmaceutical manufacturing among others.
Automotive Component orders have remained particularly strong despite earlier weakness among Automotive OEMs. While OEM orders improved in Q3, they remained 17 percent below their year-earlier level through the first nine months of 2026.
“What stands out in the third quarter is not simply the magnitude of the growth, but how broadly it was distributed across the market,” said Alex Shikany, executive vice president at A3.
“Automotive OEM orders returned to positive growth, while Automotive Components and sectors such as semiconductors/electronics and life sciences posted significant gains. That broader mix is important because it points to a robotics market that is becoming increasingly diversified across industries and applications.”
Collaborative robots also posted a strong third quarter, with 1,831 units valued at $63.8 million ordered, an increase of approximately 56 percent in units compared to Q3 2025. Collaborative robots accounted for 16.7 percent of all robot units ordered during the quarter.

items.excerpt:
Embotech and BMW Group say they have moved “1 million vehicles using automated driving technology” across four BMW Group production sites in the UK and Germany, marking a major milestone in the use of Automated Driving In-Plant in industrial production.
Automotive OEMs are increasingly turning to digitalization and automation to make production processes more efficient and flexible. Industrial automation is an important part of that shift, but much of the market remains at the pilot stage, operating only a limited number of vehicles.
The one million vehicle milestone demonstrates the scale that BMW Group has achieved with Automated Driving In-Plant, spanning different sites, brands, vehicle types and production and logistics processes.
The deployment also shows how the BMW Group and technology partner Embotech have developed Automated Driving In-Plant into a scalable solution for automated vehicle movements within the BMW Group production network.
For automated vehicle movements to become fully integrated into live production, every journey must happen with a high degree of precision and reliability. Together, BMW Group and Embotech have brought the Automated Driving In-Plant solution to approximately 3,500 vehicle movements a day, with more than 99.5 percent availability.
In production environments where unexpected downtime can disrupt wider operations, maintaining that level of availability is essential to keeping automated vehicle movements integrated into production.
Embotech provides key technology components for the Automated Driving In-Plant solution. These include Embotech’s AI-based software for perception, prediction and planning, which enables vehicles to operate in complex industrial environments, and a separate, deterministic safety architecture, independently certified by TÜV SÜD, that defines and enforces the safety boundary.
What started as an initial pilot in 2022 has now expanded to four BMW Group production sites including Dingolfing, Leipzig and Regensburg in Germany and MINI Plant Oxford in the UK.
Across the four sites, Embotech’s technology supports different automated vehicle-movement use cases in defined production and logistics areas.
For industrial operators, the value goes beyond the individual vehicle movement. Automated vehicle movements can support smoother vehicle flow, more stable and flexible operations, 24/7 capability independent of shift staffing, fewer transport damages, better use of available space and greater safety

items.title: When the Spreadsheet Stops Scaling: How to Modernize Cyclical Logistics Across Industries
items.description: Every operations team eventually outgrows the spreadsheet that got them started. A look at how to transform your monthly logistics cycle.
items.excerpt:
Somewhere in your organization, there is a spreadsheet holding things together that shouldn’t be. It was built for a smaller operation. Now it takes minutes to refresh, occasionally fails to load, and requires manual updates every cycle. Leadership lacks a clear operational view. When the person who built it leaves, institutional knowledge leaves with them.
This is not an aviation problem or a healthcare problem or a retail problem. It is an operations problem—and it shows up wherever cyclical logistics are managed at scale. The symptoms are consistent: manual vendor follow-ups, purchase orders updated by hand, no geographic visibility into where inventory actually is, and status checks that take far longer than they should.
The solution is also consistent. A recent transformation in airline in-flight entertainment (IFE) media logistics offers a clear blueprint, and the design principles translate to any supply chain managing cyclical vendor coordination.
Most operational tracking systems start with what’s available—usually a spreadsheet connected to a database. At low volume, this works. As the operation grows, the tooling does not scale with it. Refresh times slow. Columns multiply until the dashboard is unreadable. The process becomes dependent on individuals rather than systems.
The failure modes are predictable. Vendor communication happens when someone remembers to initiate it. Purchase orders are updated by hand every cycle. Status checks that should take seconds take minutes. Nobody has a real-time picture of where things stand across the network.

It appears in retail, where replenishment teams manage cyclical restocking through trackers that cannot keep pace with transaction volume. It appears in manufacturing, where MRO teams discover that critical spare parts are in the wrong facility only after a line has gone down. And it appears in logistics and freight, where shipment status across a distributed network requires manual aggregation rather than a single live view.
